title: Model Serving, Deployment Strategies and Ops
oneLiner: How a trained model answers requests, how to release a new version without breaking things, and how running ML, LLM and agent systems differs.

what.html:
Serving a model means running a fixed function: features in, prediction out. You can embed it in an app, run it as a service, run it in batches, or cache answers. New versions are released with strategies (all at once, one server at a time, switch environments, or try on a few users first) that limit damage if something is wrong. Operating models over time is MLOps; LLM apps and agents add their own concerns (LLMOps, AgentOps).

Everyday versionA restaurant tries a new dish on one table (canary), or opens a second identical kitchen and moves everyone over once it's ready (blue/green), rather than changing every cook's recipe at once (basic).

why.html:
• If serving encodes features differently from training, predictions silently go wrong.
  • The wrong serving design wastes money or adds latency.
  • A bad release should hurt as few users as possible and be quick to undo.

how.title: Inference is a fixed function
how.html: prediction = f(features, trained model). Nothing is learned at serving time: preprocess the input, call model.predict, return the answer, e.g. (5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2) → Iris-setosa.

how.title: Same encoding, always
how.html: Models only understand numbers, so raw inputs are encoded into a feature vector. Training and serving must use the very same encoding code, ideally one shared library, or the model gets inputs it never saw (training-serving skew).

how.title: Four ways to serve
how.html: Library: model inside the app. Service: a REST server many apps call. Batch: run over all data on a schedule. Cached: compute once, look up afterwards.

how.title: Releasing a new version
how.html: Basic: update everything at once (downtime, risky). Ramped: one server at a time (Kubernetes' default). Blue/green: two identical environments, flip traffic, flip back instantly if needed. Canary: a small group first, then everyone.

how.title: MLOps, LLMOps, AgentOps
how.html: MLOps runs predictive models: drift, feature stores, retraining. LLMOps runs language-model apps: prompt versions, hallucinations, token costs. AgentOps runs autonomous agents: reasoning traces, tool permissions, runaway loops, human approval.

how.title: Different systems, different metrics
how.html: ML: accuracy, F1, latency, drift. LLMs: hallucination rate, time to first token, cost per request, helpfulness. Agents: task success, tool-call correctness, number of human interventions.

demo.html: Shift the live data away from the training data and watch the population stability index (PSI) rise. Past 0.2 the MLOps loop retrains and redeploys the model.

example.html:
A recommendation service. Recommendations for all users are computed nightly (batch), and popular items are cached. A new ranking model is checked in shadow mode, then sent to 2% of users as a canary; error rates and click-through stay healthy, so a rolling update completes the rollout. The team tracks feature drift with PSI; their LLM-powered product descriptions are monitored separately for hallucinations and token cost.

Supplementary Drift doesn't always hurt accuracy. Check performance before retraining automatically, or you'll retrain more than needed.

misunderstandings: At inference the model is fixed.
Use the same code, or skew appears silently.
Blue/green limits how many users see a bug.
At the switch everyone moves; canary limits exposure.
MLOps tools are enough for agents.
Agents need trace, tool and loop monitoring too.
takeaways: prediction = f(features, fixed model); preprocessing is part of inference.
Share one encoding library between training and serving.
Serving designs: library, service, batch, cached predictions.
Deployment strategies: basic, ramped, blue/green, canary, each trading cost, speed and risk.
MLOps, LLMOps and AgentOps differ in challenges, metrics and tools; PSI-based drift detection can trigger retraining.
thirty: Inference applies a fixed trained model to encoded features, prediction = f(features, model), so the encoding code must be identical in training and serving to avoid skew. Models are served as an embedded library, a replicated REST service, scheduled batch jobs, or cached predictions. New versions are released with zero-downtime strategies: ramped replacement one node at a time, the Kubernetes default; blue/green, with two environments and an instant switch back; and canary, a small user subset first; basic all-at-once updates suit only tiny apps. MLOps covers predictive models (drift, feature stores, retraining), LLMOps covers foundation-model apps (prompts, hallucinations, token cost), and AgentOps covers autonomous agents (traces, tool authorisation, loops, human-in-the-loop), each with its own metrics. An end-to-end loop monitors drift with PSI and retrains when it exceeds a threshold.
